item.title: Calgary Stampede 2011: Interview with the paper
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: “I have a mission for you, should you chose to accept it” the Calgary Herald reporter asked over the phone. “Will my computer explode in 5 seconds if I do?” I quipped back. Her silent deadpan threw a wet blanket on what for me was a pretty sharp line, apparently she just wanted a headshot [...]
item.content:encoded:
“I have a mission for you, should you chose to accept it” the Calgary Herald reporter asked over the phone.

“Will my computer explode in 5 seconds if I do?” I quipped back.

That's me!

Her silent deadpan threw a wet blanket on what for me was a pretty sharp line, apparently she just wanted a headshot sent in for the article.  “She” being Lea Storry, perhaps the best journalist name in history.

Not used to my newfound world of press handlers and having 12 minutes of dialogue distilled into 3 sentences of sound bites, I was curious what the end result would be.  It’s more straightforward than what I’d write to tell my own story, but probably makes more sense given I answered “to get to the crossroads in the Mississippi river delta” as my motivation to sell everything I own and live in an RV.  I suppose this is my fault as I’m trying to ease into my new role with kid gloves and held back my usual quotables like “I ain’t going to work on Maggie’s farm no more” or “outer space, think about it!”

I ain't rappin for God, I ain't rappin for money

On the adjacent page in the paper is a twice as long life story of some Christian rapper Arturo Caballero who calls himself MashetiMoses, apparently given this “rap name” by God after fasting and praying.  Too bad I just finished four days of fasting in the desert and emerged named the exact same, otherwise I’d get more press.

I’m not sure if it was taken into account when selecting the Calgary Stampede 2011 intern contest winner, but you really do need to have a screw or two loose to want to live in an RV on the Stampede grounds for 10 days, and I’m in a pretty unique spot already living in an RV and being short more than a few marbles.  While writing this at the breakfast table I came to the conclusion that if I get to interview Kevin Costner, I’m going to challenge him to a kung fu battle and overdub it poorly as a short film.

Presumably the Stampede’s goal with this internship is to get as much exposure as possible, and I figure I’ll best be able to help with that if I bring a bit of edge.  But don’t worry, I’ll still be wearing pants for the TV interviews.

item.title: Ultimate Calgary Stampede Intern
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: Every day until June 17th vote for Blimpy as the Ultimate Calgary Stampede Intern! It’s a fantastic contest being run by the Calgary Stampede and if I win I get to live on the grounds for 10 days in my own trailer with 24/7 backstage access to blog about all kinds of fun and ridiculous [...]
item.content:encoded:
Every day until June 17th vote for Blimpy as the Ultimate Calgary Stampede Intern!  It’s a fantastic contest being run by the Calgary Stampede and if I win I get to live on the grounds for 10 days in my own trailer with 24/7 backstage access to blog about all kinds of fun and ridiculous stuff!  You can also watch my Calgary Stampede Intern video on YouTube, but please make sure to click the link to vote every day until June 17th.

The video itself goes through all the reasons why I think I’m qualified to show everyone a rip-roaring good time and I really appreciate everyone’s support.  Plus, you’ll be paid back in spades if I’m lucky enough to win as I promise it will be 10 days of absolute hilarity.  As the Ultimate Calgary Stampede Intern I’ll be able to cover 20 different events at the Stampede on an iPhone 4 while drafting up videos, blog posts and tweets.

Also, I’m really enjoying the chance to improve in filming and editing videos, so just think what kind of a show I can come up with when the grounds are full of people!  As you can see from the one lady at the end of my video, the Calgary Stampede seems to attract lots of excitable characters, so mix in the rodeo, some BBQ and sunny July heat and it’s guaranteed to be a great ride.

Thanks again to everyone for following Blimpy and I’d be forever grateful if you could pass the link along to anyone you can think of!

Vote Blimpy for the Ultimate Calgary Stampede Intern!

item.content:encoded:
I’m trying to get voted in as the Calgary Stampede Ultimate Social Media Intern and it would be a huge boost if people could vote for me every day from now until June 17th and repost that link wherever possible.  See the newest Blimpy video and vote for me here please!!  (Oh, and as usual it’s cooler in HD, this time only 720p…and if you want to read what the contest is for check here)

Not only will you be helping me get backstage access and my own trailer to a 10 day, 24 hour carnival of awesomeness, you’ll be helping to ensure all kinds of ridiculous content gets generated come July!

Quite the difference

The video was crafted in exactly 24 hours with my friend filming and me starring and editing.  I’m kind of a fan of the 60 second idea because it forces me to not ramble.  Also, we used a new Technicolor picture style on my camera where it films everything super flat and I have to add all the saturation, contrast and sharpness back in post, but as you can see from the before and after screenshot, I think it’s worth it and will likely be using this style for all future videos.

Also, I apologize in advance, but expect to see a lot of Facebook and Twitter updates this week reminding you to vote every day.  All we have to do is make the top 10 and the judges hand-pick a winner from there, and I legitamitly like our chances!

I hope you’re looking forward to a summer of awesomeness as much as I am!

item.title: Texas is bigger than France
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: I have had this fridge magnet since my early days working for a Texas based oil services company in 2006, and only now do I realize how true it is. While I believe it was first crafted during the “War on France” via Freedom Fries because they’re a bunch of pacifist, non-Iraqi murdering jerks, it [...]
item.content:encoded:
I have had this fridge magnet since my early days working for a Texas based oil services company in 2006, and only now do I realize how true it is.  While I believe it was first crafted during the “War on France” via Freedom Fries because they’re a bunch of pacifist, non-Iraqi murdering jerks, it also well-symbolizes the “everything is bigger in Texas” mantra, which includes Texas itself.  And you should see the Republic of Texas map from 1864, now that place was big.  However, these days whenever someone tells me I should “check out Austin because it’s cool” for the umpteenth time, a little bit of me dies inside.

Texas used to be REALLY big

The drive from Amarillo to Austin is roughly 550 miles, or in Bessie-speak $200 of gas each way, which adds up to half a month’s budget in Blimpy-speak.  I am much closer to Denver (not that I intend to go there either).  Hell, just the Texas panhandle is the same size as most states (and with less water than probably any of them too).

When I was near Sedona Arizona, for the first time I saw a weather forecast calling for “Dust”.  In Amarillo it calls for “Fire Weather”.  Not knowing what the hell this is, I Wikipedia it and find their example is a weather advisory…from Amarillo Texas.  By 7 PM I see a large smoke plume coming from a dusty dry field 10 miles away quickly spreading due to the 55 mph winds and read on the news of evacuations to the south.  The actual definition I believe is humidity below 10%, temperature above 90 F and winds greater than 40 mph.  I also realized quite suddenly around this point in time the two tornados that killed people on May 24th in Canton and Piedmont Oklahoma are only 200 miles from here, so when the skies started turning green as well, I actually got kind of nervous.

Maybe this is all happening because Repent Amarillo is right and it has nothing to do with global warming?  For the uninitiated, Repent Amarillo is an organization that deems businesses in the surrounding area immoral, then tries to shut them down with tactics ranging from calling the fire marshal to camping outside with cameras to terrorize the patrons.  I only made it to three of the spots on their map accidentally, I will investigate more when I return.

Fridge magnet FTW

I also found out the legendary “Dude, you have no Koran” was born right here in Amarillo because Repent Amarillo is apparently buddies with Terry Jones.  The facebook group Amarillo Citizens Against Repent Amarillo jumped 3500 members in one day after the event, which is not only hilarious, but uplifting that not everyone is as crazy as you think even in the so-called Bible Belt.  Although I did get a nice reply from the editor of the Amarillo Globe telling me they wouldn’t publish my letter refuting one from a pastor the day before who claimed the Bible was “undeniable scientific fact” because my retort was “too provocative”.

That said, a lot of small towns in rural Oregon and Northern California are far more horrifyingly stereotypical American than Amarillo is.  I’m convinced anywhere with at least 250,000 people must have something going on, and the Walmarts here are on the outskirts of town, have a lot less people riding motorized scooters when they can obviously walk and they sell whole wheat bread.  Honestly, the place is genuinely complex, they got layers and stuff!

item.title: Mission Accomplished: I live at a bar
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: Pulling into the mall in Amarillo and asking at a couple stores “what’s a good bar with a patio?” having spent the last week dry and fasting, I am pointed in the direction of R&R. I roll in just as the owner is opening and he gives my RV a long glare, which I view [...]
item.content:encoded:
Pulling into the mall in Amarillo and asking at a couple stores “what’s a good bar with a patio?” having spent the last week dry and fasting, I am pointed in the direction of R&R.  I roll in just as the owner is opening and he gives my RV a long glare, which I view as a bad thing, so I walk over and ask him “is this where I go to get a drink?”  He chuckles and invites me in while he gets the place ready.

I quickly learn that a bartender named Jeremy used to live in his RV that looks just like mine at the bar, parked in the same spot, which is why KC (the owner) was giving me the look.  Jeremy also just went to Santa Rosa Lake to start a few months driving to Seattle, so basically my life in reverse.  The uncanny resemblance and KC’s good natured Texan attitude had landed me a place downtown to park for as long as I want, and 5 free shots before the bar even opened to go along with the $1 draft beers.  The place got hopping for a Tuesday night with a really cool young crowd because KC explained to me to run a successful bar “you make people feel at home if they’re gay, black or purple.”  I would later discover the place is classified as a “gay bar” in Amarillo, from what I can tell because they actually let gay people in.

I started writing this from the Walmart in town I fled to after 2 days, but I’ve moved back since.  Day 1 consisted of running into the guy who worked at the mall and told me to go to R&R then drinking with his friends until the sun came up, day 2 involved enough more free shots from KC that I woke up with a pounding headache and the urge to flee.  Apparently fasting only minorly diminishes your tolerance.  Although by the time Sunday rolled around I came in to find KC with his head in his hands barely able to talk around 4:30 PM, which is just how he left the night before.  And I met two people who said “hey, Canadian guy!” claiming I had spoken with them at length earlier in the week, of which I have no recollection and I’m good at remembering faces.

After not doing it my entire trip, this time I mentally planned ahead for what I thought Texas would be like, beyond just “better than the middle of nowhere”, and my preconceptions were generally right.  Rootin tootin good times is about all I can say to sum up the attitude around here.  Screw it, let’s just have a beer, something like that.  People have tattoos that say “Don’t mess with Texas”, which is funny because the only real badge of pride in New Mexico is they serve green chile everywhere, and it’s only an hour’s drive from here.

For those that don’t know, I’m taking a break over the summer to return home to Calgary, but Amarillo will be the perfect place to return to because I’m already a regular with the local grunge crowd having met half the town at R&R and told them Jeremy’s life story even though I’ve never met him.  Hell, I even had a beer with his mom.  Also, when the daytime high is 80, it gets up to about 95 in Bessie, and it’s going to get up to 105 this week.  I’m slightly concerned things will melt when all the windows are closed while I’m gone, but as long as it doesn’t hurt the speakers I’m cool with it.

item.title: Blimpy Video #2 Explained
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: I think I said I was going to do this for the first video then never did, so considering this one’s about 500 miles more worth of footage, I figure I should at least say a few points. If you haven’t watched the vid yet, check it out here in 1080p. -When the crazy breakdown [...]
item.content:encoded:
I think I said I was going to do this for the first video then never did, so considering this one’s about 500 miles more worth of footage, I figure I should at least say a few points.  If you haven’t watched the vid yet, check it out here in 1080p.

-When the crazy breakdown starts going after the church shot about 5 minutes in, that is an abstract critique of religion.  I don’t believe the apocalypse is coming any time soon (although my timing was good with the nuts this weekend) I just kind of wanted to point out the freaky shit that happens when you let a bunch of dogmatic zealots run wild for 2000 years…creepy as hell bronze statues of the 12 stations of the cross and atom bombs.  Hell, I didn’t write The Book of Revelations, that’s why James Earl Jones reading it is sort of supposed to be out of context and creepy.

Told ya I went easy on ya

-My head was spinning after the Albuquerque Atomic museum, so I figured yours should be too, sorry if you don’t like grindcore music.  I actually went easy on you, that segment could have been twice as long and I intentionally excluded all the shots of melted bicycles that said Nagasaki, so you can thank me later.  Did you know it took 10% of the power output of the entire US from 1942 to 1945 to refine the uranium and plutonium for three bombs?

-It has been the windiest spring in 20 years in the New Mexico desert and it’s already one of the windiest places in the country, which is a) why the sound is terrible in some spots and b) why I used it to signify impending made up video doom.  The wind is blowing at 55 mph in Amarillo as I write this.

-Speaking of sound, next time I will turn my voice up.  I wanted the music to be louder as it has more punch than my ramblings, but all that did was make me hard to hear and add clipping to Mozart’s Requiem (Lacrimosa is that section in case you were wondering).  It’s hard to remember when editing that I obviously know exactly what I said so subconsciously feel it’s loud enough no matter what.

The first of several shots you never got to see. Petrified wood is 5 times harder than granite.

-I omitted several hundred really cool pictures and several potential stories from the blog starting all the way back in Arizona because I didn’t want to ruin the surprise of the intense landscapes and scenery I was experiencing.  In order they include the Petrified Forest, El Morro, El Malpais, Albuquerque, Santa Fe (and the Gearfest electronic music festival there), Cadillac Ranch and the Amarillo Botanical Gardens.  Still, uhhh, it’s the goddam desert, that’s about everything there is.  Oh, and you can’t buy alcohol for the 120 miles before Albuquerque because it’s all reservation land.

-Tucumcari itself is the largest broken down hellhole I have come across.  It’s one thing to have been cooler in 1880, and to have at one time actually been a Route 66 stop, but to still have 6000 people living there is downright depressing for them.  I didn’t take any pictures in the place because I would have got jacked for my camera.

-Here in Amarillo everything is The Good, The Bad and The Ugly themed, and a restaurant sold the Lee Van Cleff pulled pork sandwich.  I told the waitress they had misspelled it, and she disagreed, to the point I had to say “trust me, it’s Van Cleef, I would know,” while pointing at one of the movie posters on the wall to back me up.

-After Effects is a lot of fun, but takes a lot of time and computer horsepower.  That cartoon shot of me unleashing the birds took 3 hours for my computer to render into an actual watchable video file, the sand at the end about an hour and a half.  I had a full other minute worth of footage I was going to make “freaky deaky digital”, but it served no purpose other than showing what’s out there…similar to the stuff I left in.

-I totally forgot to tie back in the Hagakure reference in the cartoon segment, so I’ll end with my favourite quote from the whole book which also relates nicely to the video itself.  “When one thinks he has gone too far, he will not have erred.”

item.content:encoded:
Alright kids, fasten your seat belts because we got a brand new video out that puts the last one to shame.  If it was an appetizer, this one’s the main course, dessert and breakfast in bed the next morning.

I honestly pulled out all the stops, I got nothing left, so don’t expect another video for awhile.  I actually couldn’t sleep last night I was so excited to finish editing and publish it this morning.  My next project will be something legit, not about me and not with so much trickery.  But for now this one will more than do.

Same as last time, it’s been filmed and edited for 1080p HD, if you take the time to let it buffer and watch it in all it’s glory, you won’t be disappointed, trust me.

I take no responsibility if you have a stroke while watching.  Oh, and big shout out to the Applebee’s in Amarillo I sat at for the last 4 hours waiting for it to upload.

item.title: The Blimpy Diet!
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: Tired of exercising and watching what you eat? Try the Blimpy diet instead and just stop eating! For about 4 days, in a van, in the middle of the desert! OK, in seriousness, for reasons I can no longer remember, it seemed like an interesting plan to fast for awhile on my next trip to [...]
item.content:encoded:
Tired of exercising and watching what you eat?  Try the Blimpy diet instead and just stop eating!  For about 4 days, in a van, in the middle of the desert!

OK, in seriousness, for reasons I can no longer remember, it seemed like an interesting plan to fast for awhile on my next trip to the desert after enjoying Santa Fe.  My version of “fasting” included nothing but water with fresh lemon or lime squeezed in if desired, multivitamin pills and a couple tablespoons a day of that super raw green powder that’s made of ground up sprouts and smells and tastes like manure.

My original goal was 3 days, and I made it to 4 no problem finding each day easier than the last.  This may be related to the fact that the 40 mph winds subsided to 80 degree calm, sunny days, which makes this area quite pleasant.  This area = Santa Rosa Lake, New Mexico, FYI.

No food, no internet, no problem, we got lizards

There’s also no 3G for me to get internet here, which I’ve grown not to mind either.  I made it through Hagakure: The Way Of The Samurai, an excellent Japanese text written in 1700 made semi-famous in the movie Ghost Dog and am now settling into the Bhagavad-Gita.  Not that I’m some sort of Zen warrior, but it seems to fit the ascetic motif.  I can’t wait to get to Amarillo and explain this all to an unsuspecting Texan, tagging on to the story that I’m actually a capitalist…but that I don’t have a job and live in a van.  It all makes sense to me?

On the Zen warrior/making sense train, I will say that on day three of the fast I really did feel a great deal of clarity, sort of lighter than before, but not lightheaded.  I also slept less, and believe me, I like to sleep.  I certainly made no great revelations, nor had planned to, other than the fact that I will probably do this again sometime on my trip, it’s kind of a harmless fun way to push yourself and give the metabolism a little reset.  I imagine after about 7 days you’d start acting a bit loco though.

Being no doctor, but reading up thoroughly on the always reliable internet forums before trying this, one easily agreeable point was that I should ease back into food again, so day 5 consisted only of organic juice blends I have in the fridge, and yesterday I had two pears, a bag of snap peas, 6 stalks of celery and a dozen cherry tomatoes.  I definitely understand the logic, I’m pretty convinced that if I went straight for a McDonald’s cheeseburger right now it would clog me up so bad I would keel over and die rather promptly.  Now the challenge will be whole grains today, perhaps meat and a legitimate meal tomorrow, then all-you-can-eat Texas BBQ the day after that.  YEEHAW!!!  Amarillo actually is the birthplace of the “eat this 72 ounce steak and it’s free” promotion, I’ll be certain to stop by the joint, but not attempt it.

Best of all, I rarely ever have dreams, but the other night I honestly had one where I was at a feast in the time of King Henry VIII and there were legs of lamb and turkey drumsticks and wine and figs and apricots and the court jester danced up to me and…oh wait, didn’t I say it took until day 7 to go crazy?

Oh, there is also a lack of photos and general updates for the last while because it’s all being compiled into the next video which is 10 times more of everything than the last one, should be out within the week.

item.title: I’d like to buy a prostitute license, please
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: Santa Fe is one hell of a strange mix, and probably in the top 5 of all the cities I’ve been. Part cowboy, part yuppie, part foodie, it’s pretty hard to put a finger on, and I’ve spent more time here than anywhere in the last 2 months. For those from my part of the [...]
item.content:encoded:
Santa Fe is one hell of a strange mix, and probably in the top 5 of all the cities I’ve been.  Part cowboy, part yuppie, part foodie, it’s pretty hard to put a finger on, and I’ve spent more time here than anywhere in the last 2 months.  For those from my part of the world, think Banff, except Native themed and with actual character, not that the tourism isn’t rampant, but there’s more to it than that.

Blimpy learns how to make red chile sauce, look out

Another strange quirk is there are more raving lunatics than any place I’ve come across (eat your heart out San Francisco).  And I’m talking literal raving lunatics, everyone knows the guy in the middle of the plaza at the center of town who wears cloth wrapped around his feet for shoes and hops on one foot when he’s not crouched over muttering “sinners, sinners, sinners…”  Stranger still he’s clearly younger than me, which somewhat explains it when I bring it up with locals.  This is probably the artist capital of North America, and so while the degree to which you’ve “made it” can be measured by the distance of your gallery from the center of the very walkable downtown core, the fallacy of “I’m going to be an artist” hits all the harder when it doesn’t work out.

And as with many lines of work, the real money is in being an art dealer, the middle man.  Buy for a nickel, sell for a dime, create nothing but money in your pocket, but perhaps wear topaz and sterling silver jewellery and have a pony tail, or people here will think you are (gasp!) fake.  But believe me, the pony tailed 50 year old Western wear dealer I got my prostitute license from was the farthest from fake I have encountered in some time.

If you are ever in Santa Fe, go to the Rio Bravo Trading Company, even if you don’t need any spurs or chaps, trust me.  And if the owner Randy Rodriguez doesn’t recognize Billy Bob Thornton, Francis McDormand or the guy who plays Thor, you shouldn’t expect any special treatment in his store either.

Funny how we were more liberal 100 years ago

Seeing one of his framed prostitute licenses complete with black and white 1880s glamour shot and 5 dollar bill, I walked in to inquire on the price, but at the exact same time as one of his many old town friends.  A very weathered Native in his 60s who obviously knew Randy well, they talked family and business enough for me to gather the fellow had actually made quite the living as a bit part weathered Native in the thriving film industry here.

Once his friend left, Randy (his name is freaking Randy Rodriguez, did you pick up on that, no one on earth has a name that badass) was more than happy to tell me about how insane Republicans and people of religion are, all the celebrities and politicians he’d insulted to their face and his personal experiences with Arizona’s racist laws due to his last name despite having a bloodline in America dating back to the 1500’s.  It was really quite something and he was so most emphatically bang on I basically had to interject that I wanted to buy something from his store.

As you can see from the picture, I’d walked past the window more than once and been fascinated with Rosita del Oro.  It’s the obscured face, the mystery.  And as Randy gladly told me, a complete forgery, basically $40 for some photocopied pieces of paper and his friend’s calligraphy, but somehow to me that was one of the best deals on “art” in the entire town, and Bessie will gladly be riding with a harlot in tow for the rest of her days.
